question: If neural predictivity or representational similarity is evaluated on a system whose architecture is known, can standard neuroscience pipelines recover that architecture or its defining computational motif?

key_findings.claim: Linear neural encoding scores can misidentify even an artificial target when its exact architecture is present among the candidates.
key_findings.evidence: Using 3,000 sampled target units and cross-validated ridge readouts on six ImageNet-trained architecture families, most target layers favor the matched source, but several VGG11, ResNet18, and CORnet-S layers rank another architecture higher. A ResNet18 target can be labeled closest to recurrent CORnet-S, incorrectly suggesting recurrence; multiple matched-versus-unmatched differences are not significant at p<0.01.

anchors.section: 4.2 Identification of Architectures in an Ideal Setting

key_findings.claim: Linear CKA is more reliable for exact-model recovery in this test, yet remains insufficiently selective under realistic coverage.
key_findings.evidence: For the sampled target layers, the ground-truth source has the highest CKA, but several unmatched networks score close even when the MLP-Mixer source uses identical weights. Recomputing CKA with every target unit widens the matched-model margin, indicating that measurement coverage strongly controls identifiability.

key_findings.claim: The stimulus ensemble materially changes which architectures can be distinguished, so a score is a property of the experimental design as well as the target and candidate.
key_findings.evidence: The normalized matched-versus-unmatched identifiability index is generally higher for synthetic objects, ImageNet, and LAION images than for texture/noise stimuli and increases with target-layer depth. LAION can equal or exceed ImageNet despite all targets being ImageNet-trained, suggesting exact train-distribution matching is unnecessary. However, the texture/noise set has only 135 images versus roughly 3,000 for natural sets, leaving stimulus content partly confounded with sample count.

key_findings.claim: Functional alignment does not reliably isolate a broad architectural motif such as convolution versus attention.
key_findings.evidence: With exact target architectures removed, 12 CNN and 14 ViT variants overlap strongly for VGG13, ResNet34, and ViT-L/16 targets. At p<0.01, many target layers show no class difference—especially 7 ResNet34 and 7 ViT-L/16 layers under CKA and 6 ResNet34 layers under regression—while within-class variance is large enough that conclusions depend on the candidate sample.

anchors.section: 4.4 Challenges of Identifying Key Architectural Motifs

method.core_idea: Calibrate brain-model comparison methods on artificial systems with known ground truth, asking whether score rankings recover the exact architecture and whether they distinguish high-level architectural classes.
method.mechanism: Activations from AlexNet, VGG11, ResNet18, CORnet-S, ViT-B/32, and MLP-Mixer-B/16 serve as target recordings and candidate features. Nested-cross-validated ridge encoding reports median neuron-wise Pearson correlation; linear CKA compares population geometry. A normalized identifiability index contrasts matched-source score with the unmatched mean. Target-unit coverage, four stimulus ensembles, and a larger 12-CNN/14-ViT class test are ablated.
assumptions: Recovering the exact artificial architecture is a meaningful upper-bound test for the scientific specificity of a similarity metric.
ImageNet-trained vision networks instantiate distinct enough convolutional, recurrent, attention, and mixer motifs for identification.
Layerwise maximum matching reflects how brain regions are commonly aligned to candidate model layers.
Artificial deterministic activations with no temporal or measurement noise are favorable relative to biological recordings.
Median encoding correlation and CKA are representative of common neural-model leaderboard practice.
The selected candidate architectures adequately sample within-class variability for the motif comparison.

techniques.role: Turns an otherwise unknowable neuroscience ground truth into a controlled metric test.
Maps source-layer features to individual target units and scores held-out response correlation.
Measures population-level representational geometry without fitting per-unit readouts.
Normalizes the matched-model advantage over average unmatched models.
Tests synthetic objects, texture/noise, ImageNet, and web-natural images.
Removes the exact match and asks whether scores distinguish CNN from ViT families.

evaluations.setting: Published macaque V1/V2/V4/IT recordings in Brain-Score
evaluations.result: Markedly different ImageNet models have tightly clustered scores outside V1; VOneNet variants dominate V1 where relevant constraints were built in.
evaluations.baseline: Relative leaderboard ranking without score-separation analysis

evaluations.setting: Six artificial targets with exact architecture among candidate sources
evaluations.metric: Neuron-wise ridge correlation and linear CKA across layers
evaluations.result: Regression sometimes selects the wrong architecture; CKA selects the correct one but several alternatives are close under sampled coverage.
evaluations.baseline: Known matched architecture trained with another seed

evaluations.setting: Sampled 3,000 target units versus full target-layer coverage
evaluations.result: Full coverage substantially improves ground-truth separation, showing that recording density limits inference.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic objects, texture/noise, ImageNet, and LAION stimuli
evaluations.result: Natural or object-bearing images generally identify architectures better than texture/noise, and deeper layers are more identifiable.

evaluations.setting: 12 CNN versus 14 ViT sources for CNN and ViT targets with exact matches removed
evaluations.metric: Maximum layer score, class means, variance, and Welch tests
evaluations.result: Class score distributions overlap in many layers; broad motif recovery is sensitive to which variants enter the pool.
evaluations.baseline: Inference from the highest-scoring individual candidate

limitations: Artificial targets are deterministic, noiseless, feedforward snapshots with vastly greater observability than brains; real identifiability can only be worse under the same analysis, but may fail differently.
All principal models are visual networks trained on ImageNet, so shared data, task, and optimization may compress representational differences independently of architecture.
The exact target is deliberately placed in the source set for the main test, an unrealistically favorable closed-world assumption.
Stimulus comparisons confound content with sample count: texture/noise uses 135 images while ImageNet and LAION use about 3,000.
Layerwise maxima and testing many layers/candidates can create selection effects; the analysis does not provide a calibrated posterior over architectures or correct all model-selection multiplicity.
The identifiability index compares one true score with the mean of negatives, so a dangerous near-tie or a single higher-scoring false model can be hidden by many weak candidates.
Architecture labels are coarse: ResNets can approximate recurrence computationally, and ViTs/CNNs differ in depth, training recipe, width, and patch/token details beyond the named motif.
Only linear regression and linear CKA are deeply studied; nonlinear, task-conditioned, temporal, causal, behavioral, and intervention-based comparisons may behave differently.
Improved recovery with more units or natural images is not converted into a prospective experimental-design algorithm or validated on held-out biological hypotheses.
failure_modes: A leaderboard rewards a model whose features are easy for a linear readout to remap, not one that implements the biological computation.
A candidate pool omits the true mechanism, forcing a confidently wrong winner among equally misspecified models.
Changing the stimulus distribution reverses a model ranking and the researcher mistakes the reversal for evidence about anatomy.
Sparse recordings miss the dimensions that discriminate two candidate mechanisms.
High overall alignment masks a localized, decisive response mismatch on critical stimuli.
A metric identifies exact random-seed geometry yet fails to identify the motif scientists actually care about, or vice versa.
A flexible readout absorbs mechanistic differences and makes architectures appear equivalent.
The highest score difference is statistically detectable but too small or unstable to support a causal architectural claim.
reusable_insights: Benchmark every proposed brain-alignment metric on known synthetic systems before assigning mechanistic meaning to real-brain rankings.
Report candidate-pool sensitivity, near-ties, score uncertainty, and class-level overlap rather than only a winner.
Treat stimulus selection as experimental design and seek probes that maximize predicted disagreement among mechanisms.
Separate functional prediction, behavioral prediction, architectural constraints, temporal dynamics, and causal interventions as distinct validation axes.
Match stimulus count and information content when attributing identifiability differences to stimulus naturalness.
Measure how conclusions scale with unit coverage before extrapolating from sparse recordings.
open_questions: Can active or adversarial stimulus selection maximize information gain over mechanistic model classes under biological constraints?
Which similarity metrics recover causal computations rather than merely linearly accessible representational subspaces?
How should identifiability uncertainty be calibrated when the true architecture is outside the candidate set?
Can temporal responses, perturbations, and connectivity measurements disambiguate architectures that static encoding scores cannot?
What synthetic-system suite spans realistic noise, partial coverage, nonstationarity, recurrence, and multiple behavioral tasks?
How much target coverage is needed for a prespecified motif at a given effect size and stimulus budget?
Can task-relevant behavioral alignment predict brain-model validity better than global representational similarity?

competitive_landscape.title: Brain-Score: Which Artificial Neural Network for Object Recognition is most Brain-Like?
competitive_landscape.difference: Schrimpf et al. propose a continually updated neural and behavioral benchmark on the premise that more functionally similar networks provide better mechanistic hypotheses. The reviewed work does not dispute predictive utility, but shows that its standard scores cannot by themselves license architectural inference.

competitive_landscape.title: Controversial stimuli: pitting neural networks against each other as models of human recognition
competitive_landscape.difference: Golan et al. synthesize images that maximize disagreement among recognition models and collect human judgments, directly implementing the reviewed paper's proposed critical-stimulus direction. Their probes reveal inductive-bias differences but may be far out of natural distribution and target behavior rather than neural recordings.

competitive_landscape.title: Large-Scale Benchmarking of Diverse Artificial Vision Models in Prediction of 7T Human Neuroimaging Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Conwell et al. compare dozens of models on NSD fMRI and likewise find architecture has little effect while training task and feature reweighting matter. This real-brain breadth reinforces the reviewed warning, while not offering its known-ground-truth identifiability test.

competitive_landscape.title: Differentiable Optimization of Similarity Scores Between Models and Brains
competitive_landscape.difference: Cloos et al. directly optimize synthetic representations against neural activity under regression, CKA, and Procrustes and find score-learning dynamics can be explained by random data with matched singular spectra. This exposes metric geometry more mechanistically than candidate ranking alone.

competitive_landscape.title: Quantifying Task-relevant Similarities in Representations Using Decision Variable Correlations
competitive_landscape.difference: Qian et al. compare image-wise decoded decision variables rather than global geometry and find model-monkey task-relevant similarity below within-species ceilings and decreasing with ImageNet performance. It targets behavioral computation that the reviewed CKA/regression audit leaves open.

novelty_assessment: The known-system falsification test is the paper's strongest contribution: it converts vague concern about neural-network leaderboards into an explicit upper bound on exact-architecture and motif identifiability. The stimulus and coverage ablations make the methodological dependency concrete, while the CNN-versus-ViT test directly challenges common mechanistic interpretations. Earlier work already warned that neuroscience methods can fail on known engineered systems and large brain benchmarks observed architectural parity; this paper's novelty is joining those ideas around contemporary encoding/CKA pipelines. Its own stimulus-count confound and narrow vision setting prevent a universal verdict on neural alignment.
reviewer_notes: Read all 15 extracted pages, including metric definitions, architecture lists, brain-data comparison, artificial-target recovery, full-coverage appendix, stimulus ablations, and motif tests. Preserved the authors' glass-half-full result—identification generally improves with depth and coverage—alongside the stronger limitation on architectural inference. Five primary arXiv/bioRxiv/OpenReview works were checked on 2026-08-23.
